headline: Guilty. A jury says one man started the Palisades Fire.
summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025 that hid in tree roots for six days, then flared into the Palisades Fire. It killed 12 people and burned 6,800 buildings. His first jury deadlocked 10-2 for acquittal in June. Sentencing is March 17. Each count carries five to 20 years.

cover_question.q: Can one person start a whole fire?

cover_answer: Yes. One flame in the roots, then the wind.
table_question: If the first jury can't agree, should there be a second try?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Two winters ago a man lit a fire on a hill near Los Angeles, and the wind spread it until thousands of houses burned. Twelve grown-ups on a jury listened for days and decided he did it. A fire like that starts smaller than a birthday candle. He will be punished, and that fire is long out.
5-7.why: They hear ‘fire’ and look at the window. Say it was far away and it is long out.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes the one vivid piece, fire, and puts it at the bedroom window, so the script says far away and long out before anything else. The birthday candle makes the start small enough to picture. Cantor found this age fears what it can see. Expect ‘could it happen here?’ Say firefighters are close, and fire is a grown-up job.

8-12.script: On New Year's Day 2025 someone lit a fire on a hill above Pacific Palisades. It kept burning deep in the tree roots, and six days later the wind brought it back. It burned 6,800 buildings and killed 12 people. The jury worked a detective's board: his car at the trail, his phone on the hill, no fireworks on camera.
8-12.why: A hidden fire and a chain of clues. They can follow both to the verdict.
8-12.why_long: A twelve-year-old wants the chain to close, and this story hands over two: a fire hiding in roots for six days, and the clues that put one man on the hill. The detective's board is the mechanism, each clue a link to test. Expect ‘what if the clues are wrong?’ Say the first jury wondered too. The second saw that board and convicted.

13-17.script: Why did the second jury convict when the first voted 10-2 to acquit? Prosecutors dropped the ‘revenge on the rich’ story and stuck to his car at the trailhead, his phone on the hill, and cameras that caught no fireworks. The defense: hikers crossed the spot for six days first. Is that reasonable doubt?
13-17.why: Two juries, two answers. Let them argue it out before you rule.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold both verdicts, and the script makes them: ten jurors leaned acquit in June, twelve said guilty now, on the same fire. Kuhn calls weighing them argument practice, so let them weigh before you rule. Expect ‘so was the first jury wrong?’ Say a jury rules on what was proven, and the proof was tighter this time.

5-7.q: Can one person start a whole fire?
5-7.a: Yes. One small flame in dry grass, and the wind does the rest.

8-12.q: How could a fire hide for six days?
8-12.a: Down in the tree roots, where nobody saw it. Then the wind came.

8-12.q: How did they know it was him?
8-12.a: His car at the trail, his phone on the hill, no fireworks on camera.

13-17.q: Why did the first jury let him go?
13-17.a: It deadlocked 10-2, so no verdict. A hung jury means a retrial.
Sentencing March 17. Each count carries five to 20 years.
